text: Spread and rest both use the exact same three-dot syntax, but do opposite jobs — spread expands a collection out, rest gathers values together. Chapter Two closes with these two, since you'll see this exact syntax on nearly every page of real code from here on.

Spread expands an array's elements out, in place, inside a brand new array literal. This is the modern way to build a new array that includes an existing one's contents, without mutating the original array itself — which matters once other code elsewhere might still be holding a reference to it.

The same spread syntax works on objects too. Spreading an object and then overriding one field copies every property first, then applies just that one override — a one-line way to produce an updated copy instead of mutating the original object directly, exactly the pattern frameworks like React expect for state updates.

Rest uses the same three dots but does the opposite job: instead of expanding a collection out, it gathers any number of individual arguments into a single real array. This is how a function accepts an unknown, variable number of arguments without you having to list them all by name up front.

Rest also shows up inside destructuring — one property pulled out by name, and dot-dot-dot-rest gathering everything else that wasn't explicitly destructured into its own separate object. The rule for telling them apart: spread expands inside a literal or a function call, rest gathers inside a parameter list or a destructuring pattern.

You're ready for Chapter Three when you can use spread to produce an updated copy of an object without mutating the original, and explain how rest in a function parameter differs from spread in a function call. Spread to expand and copy without mutating, rest to gather multiple values into one array. That closes out Chapter Two. Next up: Chapter Three, asynchronous JavaScript, where every blockchain call actually happens.
